content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes a multi objective learning objective for meta learning such that each cluster learns a separate loss function to address the loss conflict among the clusters. Experimental results show the effectiveness of the proposed methods.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
**Strengths**:


* The idea of using a separate loss function for each cluster seems reasonable.  


**Weakness**:


* The assumptions that the loss among each cluster is a conflict seems not correct in practice. For example, some domains may be beneficial for each other to learn. In this case, joint training among those domains may be preferable to design separate loss functions for each cluster. 



* In terms of loss conflict, I think another alternative is to reduce gradient conflict with gradient projection, similar to [1] in multi-task learning. 


* I think there is a big computation cost for optimizing this multi-objective loss function, particularly if there are a large number of latent clusters in the dataset. 



References;

[1]  Gradient Surgery for Multi-Task Learning https://arxiv.org/abs/2001.06782 NeurIPS 2020
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The writing quality is good

The method novelty is limited as addressing the loss conflict is not new and is well-studied in existing literature. 

The results seem to be reproducible

content.summary_of_the_paper: The authors tackle the problem of few-shot learning with diverse tasks, with an emphasis on achieving stronger generalization to OOD tasks that originate from datasets not used for training. They build upon the framework of HSML, which is a MAML variant that conditions the task-specific initialization based on the cluster assignment of that task, obtained via a hierarchical clustering procedure. This paper aims to improve upon the way that the clustering is done, to obtain more ‘disentangled’ clusters (i.e clusters with less overlap), since they hypothesize that this will help with OOD tasks. They propose to achieve this using a hypervolume loss. Experimentally, they show that, compared to some previous methods, they obtain better few-shot learning performance on OOD tasks from a wide variety of domains.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths
========
[+] The proposed method seems to consistently outperform some previous work in terms of OOD task performance on a wide range of different domains.

Weaknesses
===========
[-] I found the paper hard to understand (see comments below)

[-] The experimental comparisons are against older models. It would be more relevant to compare against newer ones like SUR, URT, FLUTE, URL and the newer variant with task-specific adapters (see references below for the last two that aren't cited in this paper).

[-] I’m unsure whether the comparison to HSML is fair (as discussed below, the increase in capacity of the hierarchical clustering in the proposed method compared to HSML might be a large factor behind the increase in performance compared to HSML)?

References
==========
Universal Representation Learning from Multiple Domains for Few-shot Classification. Li et al.

Cross-domain Few-shot Learning with Task-specific Adapters. Li et al. CVPR 2022.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Clarity
=====
In the introduction, it should be clarified what are the clusters that the authors refer to (e.g. are these clusters in some learned representation space?). The narrative is hard to follow otherwise.

Figure 1 (d and e subfigures) talks about the loss on triangle shape but I don’t see any triangles in the figure (only circles, crosses and x’s). Also not sure what ‘loss on fur material’ is referring to. I think I understand the overall point of the figures but they are confusing. 

I had a hard time understanding section 4.2. What does it mean to ‘store images in the pool rather than tasks’? It sounds like the way in which tasks are created is modified in some way to have tasks that better fit the existing clusters? The next sentence talks about countering the effect of the ‘label shift’ - I’m not sure what label shift this is referring to. Is the idea to cluster based on individual images rather than clustering on tasks? This section should be rewritten to precisely describe what is proposed.

Section 4.4 is also very hard to understand, which unfortunately prevents me from understanding the proposed model. It sounds to me like the T_i ‘s are the pure and mixed tasks that have only support sets, whereas the T_o’s are the ‘objective tasks’ that have both support and query sets. I also assume that there is one T_o task per pure task, and that the support set of each T_o task exactly matches that of a pure task, with the only difference of the addition of a query set (which isn't stated in the text but I'm inferring from the figure)? But I don’t quite understand how this all fits together: how are the T_i’s used? Equation 3 is confusing because i appears on the left hand side but not the right hand side.

Figure 3c is hard to understand. It looks like all tasks are fed into ‘MAML’, not just the ‘objective tasks’? How is MAML applied on tasks that only have support sets? The 4 equations on the left hand side of that subfigure are also hard to understand. For example, what is D_o^{1q} ? 

In Equation 1, i is not defined. I’m assuming the authors meant to include a sum over different tasks.

Should give some more background and intuition about the hypervolume loss.

What exactly is the ‘reconstruction loss’? Please include an equation for this too.

The ‘pure’ and ‘mixed’ tasks aren’t really tasks (they don’t have a support and query separation and aren’t used to train the meta-learner if I understand correctly). Maybe just calling them batches is clearer. My understanding is that these are used to train the clustering but not the representation parameters.

Quality / Soundness / Correctness
==========================
In the introduction, when talking about previous work like URT and FLUTE, the authors say that ‘they require a priori the cluster a task belongs to’ - this is not an entirely accurate characterization of these methods. At test time, they don’t assume to know which dataset each task originates from. This assumption is only made at training time, so I would argue it’s not really restrictive as it’s not too hard to obtain a collection of datasets for meta-training (there are several publicly available ones).

In the first paragraph of related work, when talking about task-conditioning methods, the authors state that they fail to take the underlying clusters of tasks into consideration. This is not really true; it might be that the conditioning parameters are implicitly learning clusters of related tasks (since the idea is that similar tasks would require similar conditioning). Have the authors ran an experiment to examine this?

In preliminaries, the second equation in the paragraph describing MAML isn’t exactly accurate. In practice, we don’t sum over the gradients of the losses of all meta-training tasks in order to update the meta-parameters (we instead use a batch of meta-training tasks). The same is true of the equation in section 4.1.

Missing ablations: run standard MAML without clustering but use cut-mix for a proportion of the tasks, to imitate OOD tasks. Then, do the same for HSML. Would also be nice to incorporate cut-mix into different kinds of previous methods too, to see if this enhancement alone would yield similar results as the proposed method, though this last part may be beyond the scope of this paper.

In the experimental section, the authors mention that they increase the capacity of the hierarchical clustering model compared to HSML to better handle OOD tasks. Is the capacity increased in the same way when running HSML in these experiments? If not, a comparison should thus be made against HSML with the larger capacity, to help disentangle the gain from the added capacity from the gains of better disentangling clusters, which the proposed method aims to achieve.

Novelty
======
Throughout the paper, the authors state part of their novelty as using a multi-objective loss during training, i.e. ‘formulating multiple losses on tasks from different distributions’. This sentence describes a number of previous works too, and isn’t unique to the proposed approach. For example, SUR (Dvornik et al), URT (Liu et al) and FLUTE (Triantafillou et al), all of which are cited in this paper, can be seen as having multiple objectives too according to this description. So, I don’t think that that is where their novelty really lies. Still, the particular way of regularizing the clusters to encourage disentanglement, for the purpose of stronger OOD generalization is novel to the best of my knowledge. 

Reproducibility
============
While the authors provide values for hyperparameters and some other details, I would personally have trouble implementing this method due to my lack of clear understanding of what is proposed (see the clarity section).


Minor comments
=============
‘Different grains’ → ‘different granularities’ (in the introduction)

Figure 1b caption is ‘Illustration’ which is too general. Consider rewriting the caption.

Figure 1 caption. What does ‘inferior clustering’ refer to? If it just refers to a smaller degree of disentanglement between clusters, it should just be called that. 

‘a variant donated’ → ‘a variant denoted’ (in the ‘Ablation study’ paragraph)
content.summary_of_the_review: Overall, it seems that the proposed method yields improvements over some previous methods for the case of OOD tasks. I’m not sure how it would fare against newer methods that were developed for this problem. I also found the paper hard to understand and some parts of the proposed method remain unclear to me after reading several times. Therefore, I recommend rejection of the paper in its current form.
content.correctness: 3: Some of the paper’s claims have minor issues. A few statements are not well-supported, or require small changes to be made correct.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 3: The contributions are significant and somewhat new. Aspects of the contributions exist in prior work.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper introduces the multi-objective optimization method to meta learning. The proposed method has been shown to improve the meta-generalization capability.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:

+ The perspective on using MOO to improve the meta generalization of meta learning is novel and interesting.
+ The empirical results are promising.

Weaknesses:
+ The proposed method seems incremental.
+ The paper is in general hard to follow.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Clarity: The writing needs to be improved in order to make the logic of this paper easily understood.

Quality: Fairly good.

Novelty: The technical novelty seems to be limited. 

Reproducibility: Good.
content.summary_of_the_review: This paper studies an interesting perspective on improving meta generalization and extensive experiments are done to verify the proposed method. However, the technical novelty looks rather limited as this paper seems to merely borrow some idea from MOO to meta learning. Moreover, the writing of this paper needs to be improved to help readers better understand the details and the main logic.
